I rolled over in bed, listening to the sound of my pager going off. It couldn’t have been more than 15 minutes since I had dropped into bed from my last admission. I looked at the number on the pager. Yes, it was the Emergency Department again.

I attempted to rub the sleep out of my eyes and stir my still sleepy brain to wakefulness. I picked up the phone and dialed the ER. “Hey,” the ER doctor said. “I’ve got two admissions for you.”

“Oh,” I said sleepily.

“You sound tired,” he said, jokingly.

I was tired. After graduating from Medical School, doctors go through an intense training period called residency. The first two years of that training period involved overnight calls in the hospital. It wasn’t unusual to put in one hundred hours at the hospital in a week’s time.

Even when we weren’t on call, the days started early and went late. I often fought sleep as I was driving home from the hospital. I certainly learned a lot during that time, but I am also glad that those days are behind me.

Fatigue is part of the human condition. Everyone has had times when they struggled with tiredness. Maybe it was due to a job that needed to get done, a long trip, or sleepless nights due to a new baby in the family—whatever the difficulty, we determinedly push ourselves to make it through these challenging times.

From our childhood days we are taught that work is important. We need to be responsible and take care of the tasks that are set for us to do.

Work is ordained by God. In Genesis Chapter 2, God gave Adam the task of caring for the Garden of Eden. Later, in Deuteronomy 5:13, the Israelites were commanded to do all their work in six days and then rest the seventh day.

The New Testament gives a couple of more reasons to work. We are to work so we can provide for our families (see II Thessalonians 3:10). In addition, we are to work so we can give to others who are in need (see Ephesians 4:28).

God expects us to work and that we do it in a way that will glorify Him. However, we also have need of rest, which God made provision for as well.

God Exemplified Rest in the Creation

And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made –Genesis 2:2-3.

When God created the universe, including the earth and all it contains, it took Him just six days. Since God is God, we can be certain that He wasn’t tired at the end of this work. Yet, despite that fact, He took a day of rest and set it apart. He did it as an example for us.

Even though the law of the Sabbath would not be instituted for at least two thousand years, the precedent was set in Creation… Rest one day a week.

God Mandated Rest in the Law

Perhaps the thing that comes to mind first is the Sabbath Day laws that were given in Exodus 20:8-11. It was specifically commanded that the people were not to work on the Sabbath. And further, they were not to cause other people to work either.

Another law which seemed very much focused on the need for rest was the Year of Jubilee. In Leviticus 25, this law mandated that every seven years the land was to lie fallow for the whole year, slaves were to be released, land was to revert to its original family’s ownership, and debts were to be cancelled.

Within the Jubilee commands were certain promises. There was the promise of freedom—no matter how bad things had been the previous six years there would be a reset. It was a promise of inheritance—the things that had been lost and sold would be reclaimed. It was a promise of abundance—And if ye shall say, What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase: Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years –Leviticus 25:20-21. Most of all, it was a promise of rest from labor—for the people and the land.

These commands were not put on the people to afflict them. Rather, God gave them knowing that without them His people would not rest enough and would not take enough time to focus on Him, their Creator.

Each one of us needs times of rest, but we need to understand that keeping the Sabbath is not simply about abstinence from work. Our efforts at keeping the Sabbath must include both rest and worship and it must be emphasized with the presence of God in our lives, without distraction.

The New Testament did not Change the Need for Rest

One of the verses that comes to my mind when I think about rest, is a promise that Jesus gave. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light –Matthew 11:28-30.

The biblical book of Hebrews also speaks of the importance of rest and of our entering into God’s rest. There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief –Hebrews 4:9-11.

It is important to see that the New Testament concept of rest is more than simply time off from work. True biblical peace is intrinsically intertwined with the concept of peace, even in the midst of a chaotic world. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid –John 14:27. Jesus gave peace to His followers that allowed them to be at rest, even when they were dealing with high levels of stress.

This is a blessing, for it is not enough simply to take time off from our normal work. We need to have that peace and calm which a connection with Jesus offers. Without …the peace of God, which passeth all understanding… –Philippians 4:7, our time off will be just as unrestful as our time at work.

It is clear that God wants us to rest. He knows that we need it, not just for spiritual reasons, but also for our physical health.

******************************

The folks in charge of the French Revolution made an attempt to eliminate all the institutions of the past. It was a particularly godless endeavor and among other things, the new government decided to “reform” the calendar.

In 1793, they established a ten-day work week. Each month would have three weeks with one rest day in each of these ten-day weeks. Their goal, among other things, was to eliminate all religious holidays and the celebration of Sunday as a day of rest. They believed that more work would be done by having fewer days of rest each month.

This created a huge headache for watchmakers. They needed to somehow make watches that would support the details of these new decrees—each day would be ten hours long, each hour would contain one hundred minutes, and each minute would be 100 seconds long.

It turned out to be a disaster. The people hated the changes and productivity dropped considerably across France. Finally, in 1806, Napoleon abolished it and went back to the old calendar and the system of Sunday days of rest. This scientific “experiment” was over. It turns out that people need times of rest and recharging and that a seven-day week with one day off to rest is not just a Christian concept, it is something that is necessary for health and wellbeing.

The Soviet Union, under Joseph Stalin, also tried a similar experiment of eliminating Sunday rest, with similar results.

******************************

The week, as God created it, (with one day in seven for rest) is necessary for us to remain productive.

Rest Reduces Inflammation

Part of the problem that modern people face is that they deal with high levels stress hormones, like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones increase blood pressure and pulse rates. They also increase levels of inflammation in our bodies.

Chronic inflammation is not healthy, but fortunately, rest really seems to help bring those hormone levels down a lot. A good night of sleep is essential for healing, precisely because it turns down these hormones and allows healing of overworked nerves and tissues.

Autoimmune diseases and pain levels improve when people get adequate levels of sleep. Blood pressure and heart conditions also benefit when a person gets adequate amounts of restorative sleep.

Rest Allows for Healing

Exercise is a good thing. Doctors recommend doing regular cardiovascular exercise because it is healthy for our hearts, minds, and overall wellbeing.

It is not wise to exercise every day. It too, raises stress hormone levels and does not give our bodies adequate times to heal. People who exercise too frequently and with too much intensity are much more likely to end up with nagging injuries, joint and muscle pain, and fatigue. One study found that it takes 72 hours after doing weight training for muscles to fully recover.

People who exercise ideally need one to two days off a week to let their bodies recover from the activity. The harder you are training, the more you need those times of rest. Even someone who is training intensively for something like a marathon needs to take periodic days with no running or they will injure themselves.

Rest Decreases Pain Levels

There have been many studies that looked at people’s reports of sleep and looked at things like chronic pain and tension headaches. At least 50 percent of people with insomnia also have chronic pain. Of course, it could simply be that people with chronic pain don’t sleep as well as people who don’t have that.

There have been several studies that looked at people’s pain tolerance after sleep deprivation. They found that even a single night of sleep deprivation was enough to make people feel pain more acutely.

Rest Improves Our Immune Systems

There have been several studies that looked at function of different parts of our immune systems and found that they work better when study participants have adequate levels of sleep. Probably the fact that inflammation levels are higher when we don’t rest, increases the risks of infection.

When we push ourselves too hard without rest it is hard on our immune systems. On the other hand, the best way to recover is to make certain that we get sufficient rest.

There are many other things that rest does. It helps improve mood. It can help with academic performance and memory tasks.

As with all things, moderation is key. Someone who does nothing but rest and sleep, is not going to have any better function than someone who sleeps well for seven hours a night, nor will they be very productive.

There are some basic rules that can help us with times of rest.

Rest Regularly

The message of the Sabbath is that we need to take regular, short periods of time to rest. The Jubilee Years tell us that we need less frequent, longer times to recharge. It takes effort and scheduling to make certain that these times are truly restful.

Maybe it is a bit like a car. You can only drive so far on a tank of gas. If you always wait until the warning light turns on to fill up that tank, eventually you will have this happen when you are too far from a gas station to fill up before you run out of gas. There is never a good time to run out of gas. In the same way, we need to periodically recharge our spiritual, emotional, and physical batteries. There is no reason to wait until warning signs show up that we desperately need to take a break.

Rest Takes Preparation

The story of the gift of manna in Exodus 16 tells us that manna came every day. The people could not keep it for a second day because it would spoil. However, on Fridays, they were to gather extra since the next day was a day of rest and no manna came on the Sabbath. Those who had not gathered extra the day before went hungry.

In the same way, it takes preparation to have these sorts of times. It won’t be easy, but it is important.

Do Healthy Things With Your Rest

There is a tendency when people are under stress to eat unhealthy things. When people are exhausted, they don’t usually feel like exercising or taking walks. These are the sorts of things that can really help recharge us, both physically and emotionally.

Once again, this takes some effort, but choosing healthy options is important for our well-being.

Focus on God

I have left this till the last, but it is the most important aspect of rest. True rest grows, not out of medication or even multiple vacations, but out of a heart that is filled with peace. The peace which passes understanding comes from a heart that is focused on God.

Our times of prayer and Bible reading should be times of rest. If we can eliminate distractions and the challenges of our work and home life and train our gaze on the One who matters most, we will receive a real blessing and the recharging that our spirits need.

I am afraid that many people struggle to find rest because they are not truly at peace. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief –Hebrew 4:11. The rest here is one that is promised to those who persevere and receive God’s peace.

Conclusion

Life is about balance. There are times when we need to work and there are times as well when we should rest. Figuring out this balance is the challenge which each of us faces. What is certain, is that every 24-hour day will be completely full by the time we get to the end of it.

God sees us and our limitations and desires for us to achieve this balance between our work and our times of rest. If we can only focus ourselves on Him, we will receive guidance in this balance.

Most of all, we will receive a peace that is without price, that will allow us to find rest—even during a storm.

Me di la vuelta en la cama al oír que sonaba mi localizador. No podían haber pasado más de 15 minutos desde que me había metido en la cama después de mi último ingreso. Miré el número que aparecía en el localizador. Sí, era otra vez el Servicio de Urgencias.

Intenté quitarme el sueño de los ojos y despertar mi cerebro, todavía adormecido. Tomé el teléfono y llamé a Urgencias. —Hola —dijo el médico de Urgencias—. Tengo dos ingresos para ti.

—Ah —respondí con voz soñolienta.

—Suena cansado —dijo en tono de broma.

Estaba cansado. Después de graduarse de la facultad de Medicina, los médicos pasan por un período de formación intensiva llamado residencia. Los dos primeros años de esa formación incluían guardias nocturnas en el hospital. No era raro trabajar cien horas en el hospital en una semana.

Incluso cuando no estábamos de guardia, los días empezaban temprano y terminaban tarde. A menudo luchaba contra el sueño mientras conducía de regreso a casa desde el hospital. Sin duda aprendí mucho durante ese tiempo, pero también me alegra que esos días hayan quedado atrás.

La fatiga es parte de la condición humana. Todos hemos pasado por momentos en que nos cuesta vencer el cansancio. Quizá se debiera a un trabajo que había que terminar, a un viaje largo o a noches sin dormir por la llegada de un bebé a la familia; sea cual sea la dificultad, nos esforzamos con determinación para superar esos momentos difíciles.

Desde pequeños nos enseñan que el trabajo es importante. Debemos ser responsables y ocuparnos de las tareas que se nos encomiendan.

El trabajo ha sido ordenado por Dios. En Génesis, capítulo 2, Dios le dio a Adán la tarea de cuidar el huerto del Edén. Más adelante, en Deuteronomio 5:13, se les ordenó a los israelitas que hicieran todo su trabajo en seis días y que descansaran el séptimo.

El Nuevo Testamento ofrece un par de razones más para trabajar. Debemos trabajar para poder mantener a nuestras familias (véase 2 Tesalonicenses 3:10). Además, debemos trabajar para poder dar a quienes tienen necesidad (véase Efesios 4:28).

Dios espera que trabajemos y que lo hagamos de una manera que lo glorifique. Sin embargo, también necesitamos descansar, y Dios dispuso que así fuera.

Dios dio el ejemplo del descanso en la creación

Y acabó Dios en el día séptimo la obra que hizo; y reposó el día séptimo de toda la obra que hizo. Y bendijo Dios al día séptimo, y lo santificó: porque en él reposó de toda la obra que había creado y hecho –Génesis 2:2-3.

Cuando Dios creó el universo, incluida la tierra y todo lo que contiene, lo hizo en solo seis días. Puesto que Dios es Dios, podemos estar seguros de que no estaba cansado al terminar esta obra. Sin embargo, a pesar de eso, se tomó un día de descanso y lo apartó. Lo hizo para darnos ejemplo.

Aunque faltaban al menos dos mil años para que se instituyera la ley del sábado, el precedente quedó establecido en la creación… Descansar un día a la semana.

Dios estableció el descanso en la ley

Quizá lo primero que viene a la mente sean las leyes sobre el día de reposo dadas en Éxodo 20:8-11. Se ordenó específicamente que el pueblo no trabajara en sábado. Además, tampoco debían hacer trabajar a otras personas.

Otra ley que parecía centrarse mucho en la necesidad de descansar era la del año del jubileo. En Levítico 25, esta ley establecía que cada siete años la tierra debía quedar en barbecho durante todo el año, los esclavos debían ser liberados, la tierra debía volver a ser propiedad de la familia a la que originalmente pertenecía y las deudas debían ser canceladas.

Los mandatos del jubileo incluían ciertas promesas. Estaba la promesa de libertad: por muy mal que hubieran sido las cosas durante los seis años anteriores, habría un nuevo comienzo. Era una promesa de herencia: se recuperarían las cosas que se habían perdido y vendido. Era una promesa de abundancia: Y si dijereis: ¿Qué comeremos el año séptimo? he aquí no hemos de sembrar, ni hemos de recoger nuestros frutos: Entonces yo os enviaré mi bendición el sexto año, y ella hará fruto por tres años –Levítico 25:20-21. Pero, sobre todo, era una promesa de descanso del trabajo, para el pueblo y para la tierra.

Estos mandatos no se impusieron al pueblo para afligirlo. Más bien, Dios se los dio porque sabía que, sin ellos, su pueblo no descansaría lo suficiente ni dedicaría suficiente tiempo a centrarse en Él, su Creador.

Cada uno de nosotros necesita momentos de descanso, pero debemos entender que guardar el sábado no consiste simplemente en abstenerse de trabajar. Nuestros esfuerzos por guardar el sábado deben incluir tanto el descanso como la adoración, y debe destacarse la presencia de Dios en nuestra vida, sin distracciones.

El Nuevo Testamento no cambió la necesidad de descansar

Uno de los versículos que me viene a la mente cuando pienso en el descanso es una promesa que dio Jesús. Venid a mí todos los que estáis trabajados y cargados, que yo os haré descansar. Llevad mi yugo sobre vosotros, y aprended de mí, que soy manso y humilde de corazón; y hallaréis descanso para vuestras almas. Porque mi yugo es fácil, y ligera mi carga –Mateo 11:28-30.

El libro bíblico de Hebreos también habla de la importancia del descanso y de entrar en el reposo de Dios. Por tanto, queda un reposo para el pueblo de Dios. Porque el que ha entrado en su reposo, también él ha reposado de sus obras, como Dios de las suyas. Procuremos pues de entrar en aquel reposo; que ninguno caiga en semejante ejemplo de desobediencia –Hebreos 4:9-11.

Es importante ver que el concepto de descanso en el Nuevo Testamento es más que simplemente tomarse un tiempo libre del trabajo. La verdadera paz bíblica está intrínsecamente entrelazada con el concepto de la paz, incluso en medio de un mundo caótico. La paz os dejo, mi paz os doy: no como el mundo la da, yo os la doy. No se turbe vuestro corazón, ni tenga miedo –Juan 14:27. Jesús dio a sus seguidores una paz que les permitía descansar, incluso cuando enfrentaban niveles elevados de estrés.

Esto es una bendición, pues no basta con tomarnos tiempo libre de nuestro trabajo habitual. Necesitamos esa paz y esa calma que ofrece la conexión con Jesús. Sin …la paz de Dios, que sobrepuja todo entendimiento… –Filipenses 4:7, nuestro tiempo libre será tan poco reparador como el tiempo que pasamos trabajando.

Está claro que Dios quiere que descansemos. Él sabe que lo necesitamos, no solo por razones espirituales, sino también por nuestra salud física.

******************************

Los responsables de la Revolución francesa intentaron eliminar todas las instituciones del pasado. Fue una iniciativa particularmente impía y, entre otras cosas, el nuevo gobierno decidió «reformar» el calendario.

En 1793, establecieron una semana laboral de diez días. Cada mes tendría tres semanas, con un día de descanso en cada una de esas semanas de diez días. Entre otros objetivos, querían eliminar todas las fiestas religiosas y la celebración del domingo como día de descanso. Creían que se trabajaría más si había menos días de descanso cada mes.

Esto les causó un gran problema a los relojeros. De alguna manera tenían que fabricar relojes que se ajustaran a los detalles de estos nuevos decretos: cada día duraría diez horas, cada hora tendría cien minutos y cada minuto duraría 100 segundos.

Resultó ser un desastre. A la gente no le gustaron los cambios y la productividad cayó considerablemente en toda Francia. Finalmente, en 1806, Napoleón abolió el sistema y volvió al calendario antiguo y al sistema de descanso dominical. Este «experimento» científico había terminado. Resulta que las personas necesitan períodos de descanso y recuperación, y que una semana de siete días con un día libre para descansar no es solo un concepto cristiano: es algo necesario para la salud y el bienestar.

La Unión Soviética, bajo el mando de Joseph Stalin, también intentó un experimento similar para eliminar el descanso dominical, con resultados parecidos.

******************************

La semana tal como Dios la creó (con un día de descanso de cada siete) es necesaria para que sigamos siendo productivos.

El descanso reduce la inflamación

Parte del problema que enfrentan las personas de hoy es que tienen niveles elevados de hormonas del estrés, como la adrenalina y el cortisol. Estas hormonas aumentan la presión arterial y la frecuencia del pulso. También aumentan los niveles de inflamación en nuestro cuerpo.

La inflamación crónica no es saludable, pero, por fortuna, el descanso parece ayudar mucho a reducir esos niveles hormonales. Dormir bien por la noche es esencial para sanar, precisamente porque reduce estas hormonas y permite que sanen los nervios y tejidos sobreexigidos.

Las enfermedades autoinmunes y los niveles de dolor mejoran cuando las personas duermen lo suficiente. La presión arterial y las afecciones cardíacas también se benefician cuando una persona duerme lo suficiente y obtiene un sueño reparador.

El descanso permite sanar

Hacer ejercicio es bueno. Los médicos recomiendan hacer ejercicio cardiovascular con regularidad porque es saludable para el corazón, la mente y el bienestar general.

No es prudente hacer ejercicio todos los días. También eleva los niveles de hormonas del estrés y no da a nuestro cuerpo tiempo suficiente para sanar. Quienes hacen ejercicio con demasiada frecuencia y demasiada intensidad tienen muchas más probabilidades de acabar con lesiones persistentes, dolores articulares y musculares, y fatiga. Un estudio encontró que los músculos tardan 72 horas en recuperarse por completo después de hacer entrenamiento con pesas.

Lo ideal es que quienes hacen ejercicio descansen uno o dos días a la semana para que el cuerpo se recupere de la actividad. Cuanto más intenso sea el entrenamiento, más se necesitan esos períodos de descanso. Incluso alguien que entrena intensamente para algo como un maratón necesita tomarse días periódicos sin correr, o se lesionará.

El descanso reduce el dolor

Se han realizado muchos estudios que examinaron los informes de las personas sobre el sueño y analizaron aspectos como el dolor crónico y las cefaleas tensionales. Al menos el 50 por ciento de las personas con insomnio también tienen dolor crónico. Por supuesto, es posible que simplemente las personas con dolor crónico no duerman tan bien como quienes no lo padecen.

Varios estudios analizaron la tolerancia al dolor de las personas después de privarlas del sueño. Descubrieron que una sola noche sin dormir bastaba para que las personas sintieran el dolor con mayor intensidad.

El descanso mejora nuestro sistema inmunitario

Varios estudios analizaron el funcionamiento de diferentes partes de nuestro sistema inmunitario y descubrieron que funcionan mejor cuando los participantes duermen lo suficiente. Probablemente, el hecho de que los niveles de inflamación sean más altos cuando no descansamos aumenta el riesgo de infección.

Cuando nos exigimos demasiado sin descansar, nuestro sistema inmunitario se resiente. Por otro lado, la mejor manera de recuperarnos es asegurarnos de descansar lo suficiente.

El descanso tiene muchos otros efectos. Ayuda a mejorar el estado de ánimo. Puede ayudar con el rendimiento académico y las tareas de memoria.

Como con todo, la moderación es clave. Alguien que no hace más que descansar y dormir no funcionará mejor que alguien que duerme bien siete horas por noche, y tampoco será muy productivo.

Hay algunas reglas básicas que pueden ayudarnos a descansar.

Descansar con regularidad

El mensaje del sábado es que necesitamos tomarnos períodos breves y regulares para descansar. Los años del jubileo nos enseñan que también necesitamos períodos más largos y menos frecuentes para recuperarnos. Hace falta esfuerzo y planificación para asegurarnos de que esos momentos sean verdaderamente reparadores.

Quizá sea un poco como un automóvil. Solo puedes conducir cierta distancia con un tanque de gasolina. Si siempre esperas a que se encienda la luz de advertencia para llenar el tanque, tarde o temprano te ocurrirá cuando estés demasiado lejos de una gasolinera para cargar combustible antes de quedarte sin gasolina. Nunca es buen momento para quedarse sin gasolina. Del mismo modo, necesitamos recargar periódicamente nuestras baterías espirituales, emocionales y físicas. No hay razón para esperar a que aparezcan señales de advertencia de que necesitamos desesperadamente tomarnos un descanso.

El descanso requiere preparación

El relato del regalo del maná en Éxodo 16 nos dice que el maná llegaba todos los días. El pueblo no podía guardarlo para el día siguiente porque se echaba a perder. Sin embargo, los viernes debían recoger una cantidad adicional, ya que el día siguiente era de descanso y no caía maná en sábado. Quienes no habían recogido más el día anterior pasaban hambre.

Del mismo modo, hace falta prepararse para tener este tipo de períodos. No será fácil, pero es importante.

Aprovecha el descanso para hacer cosas saludables

Cuando las personas están estresadas, tienden a comer cosas poco saludables. Cuando están agotadas, por lo general no tienen ganas de hacer ejercicio ni de salir a caminar. Sin embargo, esas son precisamente algunas de las cosas que pueden ayudarnos mucho a recargarnos, tanto física como emocionalmente.

Una vez más, esto requiere cierto esfuerzo, pero elegir opciones saludables es importante para nuestro bienestar.

Centrarse en Dios

He dejado esto para el final, pero es el aspecto más importante del descanso. El verdadero descanso no nace de los medicamentos ni siquiera de tomarse varias vacaciones, sino de un corazón lleno de paz. La paz que sobrepasa el entendimiento proviene de un corazón centrado en Dios.

Nuestros momentos de oración y lectura de la Biblia deberían ser momentos de descanso. Si podemos eliminar las distracciones y las preocupaciones de nuestra vida laboral y familiar, y fijar la mirada en Aquel que más importa, recibiremos una verdadera bendición y la renovación que nuestro espíritu necesita.

Me temo que a muchas personas les cuesta encontrar descanso porque no tienen verdadera paz. Procuremos pues de entrar en aquel reposo; que ninguno caiga en semejante ejemplo de desobediencia –Hebreos 4:11. El descanso al que aquí se alude es el que se promete a quienes perseveran y reciben la paz de Dios.

Conclusión

La vida se trata de equilibrio. Hay momentos en que necesitamos trabajar y también hay momentos en que debemos descansar. Encontrar ese equilibrio es el desafío que todos enfrentamos. Lo que sí es seguro es que cada día de 24 horas estará completamente ocupado cuando llegue a su fin.

Dios nos ve, conoce nuestras limitaciones y desea que alcancemos este equilibrio entre el trabajo y nuestros momentos de descanso. Si logramos centrarnos en Él, recibiremos orientación para encontrar ese equilibrio.

Sobre todo, recibiremos una paz que no tiene precio y que nos permitirá descansar, incluso durante una tormenta.

I’ll walk with God—Today—
Tomorrow may not be.
I’ll make the best of TIME—right now—
That God has granted me.

I’ll plan not for a life
That I might live in ease,
But only for today to live
My God alone to please.

Nor dare I think in years
Or move from leaps to bounds;
With God shut out, and self shut in
And selfish aims surround.

There are those who plan their lives,
Who give God little thought;
Who weigh themselves, not with God’s truth,
As every day they ought!

“Boast not thyself,” I’m warned,
“Of what tomorrow brings;
Thy health and wealth—e’en life itself—
May all at once take wings!”

“This night, that soul of thine
May be required of thee:
And dost thou plan the New Year full
There, ‘neath some Christmas tree?”

“Wake up! Take stock, are you prepared?
Your lessons learned alright?
If God, in yet three hours, THIS DAY,
Should close your course TONIGHT?”

Ek sal vandag met God wandel—
Môre bestaan dalk nie.
Ek sal die meeste maak van TYD—nou dadelik—
Wat God my geskenk het.

Ek sal nie beplan vir ’n lewe

Ek durf ook nie in jare dink
Of met reusespronge vooruitbeur nie;

En selfsugtige oogmerke wat my omring.

Daar is dié wat hul lewens beplan,
Wat min aan God dink;
Wat hulself nie aan God se waarheid meet nie,
Soos hulle elke dag behoort te doen!

“Moenie roem nie,” word ek gewaarsku,

kan alles skielik wegvlieg!”

“Vanaand kan daardie siel van jou

onder ’n Kersboom?”

jou lewensloop VANAAND sou afsluit?”

Thou hast the dew of thy youth. Psalm 110:3

There are many aspects of youth which are not virtuous. Many youth of our day experience an early season of callused carelessness and casualty. Often decisions that are made in youthful years set the foundation for the rest of their lives. It was a the younger prodigal brother that asked for an early draw on his inheritance then went and wasted it on riotous living. It was a young Dinah who wandered from her father’s house and …went out to see the daughters of the land –Genesis 34:1. There, she was exposed to the heathen young men of the land and occasioned a bloody massacre, leaving Jacob as a stench in the land. Many foolish young people have sown to the wind and reaped the havoc thereof. Those that are void of solid principles and parental authority are at high risk for spiritual shipwreck.

There are particular lusts that inflict youth more so than the aged, and the young are exhorted to flee them. (–see 2 Timothy 2:22) Solomon looked through his window casement, And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding -Proverbs 7:6-7. The young man was in heartfelt pursuit of that which appeared lovely… [Un]Till a dart [struck] through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life –Proverbs 7:23. We could examine the vices from the youthful lives of Rehoboam, Amnon, Nadab and Abihu, and countless others. We also find no lack of modern, folly-filled examples about us fulfilled by frivolous youth.

But youth are not meant to be despised. Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity –1 Timothy 4:12. In fact, God generally chooses the youth as the instruments of His propagation. Joseph, of sterling character, was sent by God into Egypt at the age of 17 to preserve life (–see Genesis 45:5). Miriam, at the age of twelve, stood post over the future deliverer of the entire Jewish nation and secured her own mother, Jochebed, to be the nurse of the baby Moses. David, as a youth, was sent to encourage his brethren in the army. He was despised by his brothers: …I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart… –1 Samuel 17:28. He was rejected by Saul: …Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth… –1 Samuel 17:33. He was scorned by Goliath: …Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves… –1 Samuel 17:43. But their contempt was all for naught when he was chosen by God to be king over all Israel.

These noble youthful ambitions were followed by Josiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Mary, and the disciples of the Lord, all who chose to remember their Creator in the days of their youth. But these were not naive specimens seeking to secure their place in life, they were graphic examples of youth who were seeking to imitate the image of their Lord.

We need not gaze long into the character of Christ before we find…

...Thou hast the dew of thy youth

Psalm 110 is perhaps the most referred-to scripture in the Old Testament. This rhetorical portrait of the Messiah reveals a vivid virtue for us to behold. Christ, as the Ancient of days, was described in the Revelation having His head and His hairs ... white like wool, as white as snow… –Revelation 1:14, yet, here He is depicted as eternally young, as He sits at the right hand of God (–see Psalm 110:1). No weariness of age can enter there, for Christ is the Morning Star. It is perpetual morning around the throne of God. Those saints who are following hard after His likeness will also reflect this virtue, for the light of Jesus is the light of youth.

The psalmist, describing the Messiah, draws from the natural beauty of the morning dew (–see Psalm 110:3). The thought of dew calls us back from the heavens and unveils before us a portrait of this earth on which we dwell. In heaven there is no night, no change of heat and cold, no need of the sun to light up the day and consequently… no dew. The nature of dew belongs to the terrestrial, where everyone who will but stoop to observe it will behold a uniformed regiment of grass sparkling as if embedded with a myriad of diamonds. After a long night of darkness, the dewdrops, like tears, stand in the eyes of the flowers as they weep for joy at the advent of the first morning sunbeam. Those who walk through the lowly vegetation will have their feet washed by a thousand caressing hands of God’s design. Christ is not depicted as the dew of the morning but as the dew of youth, and the imagery is stretched further.

Youth is the season of abounding energy. Some cannot sit still. They are generally interpersonal creatures who love social activity. This is neither a virtue nor a vice. Rather, it is nominal nature. There is a progressive strain in advancing years that tames and tempers the soul. As life progresses, there is a clearer vision and a steadier thought, and we rise to better things. But when the mid-life summit has been crossed and the feet are traveling downward on the slope, that tumultuous rush of bodily energy that plowed through anything becomes enshrined with memories of the past. It is the closest comfort many can find to the bygone days of their strength.

But Christ has not called us to foster a fondness for the past nor a wistful longing for the “DO” of our youth. So many today sadly lament that their ‘get-up-and-go’ has got up and went. These have no vision for higher things and are more energized by a can of Mountain Dew than the Dew of Youth. They are more inspired by a trip down memory lane and reminiscing events of the past than of the hope that lies before them.

Age is no hindrance to securing the dew of youth. The Ancient of Days still rides forth among the golden candlesticks. While John beheld His hairs ... white like wool, as white as snow… –Revelation 1:14, yet Solomon declares …his locks are bushy, and black as a raven –Song of Solomon 5:11. While age may steal our strength and hearing, …the LORD’S hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear: –Isaiah 59:1. He has secured the dew of youth and invites us to partake. The problem is not found in our deteriorating body but in a spiritually declining mind. The bane of old age predominately sets in when the mind follows the body.

It is not that life grows poorer as it advances or ceases to be noble when the charm of youth has faded. If we were placed here only to experience joy, the dying out of youthful romance would be terrible. God had a much greater end in view for His children than to just be vibrant ‘doers’. We are sent here to learn. Our allotted years upon earth are all meant to be a schooling, and it is not in the bright romance of youth that we learn the best and most abiding lessons. It is in the dogged doing of our duty, the quiet acceptance of our limitations, the patient carrying of our daily burden, and in the stretching out of a helping hand to our brother. These afford us the true opportunities for Christian culture and are the roots of ethical nobility. Christ labored …not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life… –John 6:27, and He finished His earthly task in 33 years. But the dew of youth did not dissipate as He sat down at the right hand of His Father.

Thus, we conclude that this youthfulness will not be secured by strength, but by…

...Hope

But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God; From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. –Hebrews 10:12-13.

How shall we picture this Christ now? Reclining in an easy chair, all worn out from His experience with the stubborn people of this earth? Is He busy putting together a scrap book of precious memories? This is too often the position of the aged and so their mind dies with their bodies.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope –Romans 5:3-4. At times, we wonder if this scripture can be true. Anyone with any age on their bones can testify to a poor experience and the subsequent feelings of hopelessness following. As people, we have all faced disappointing experiences with a spouse, a child, or a church relationship after which a nagging cloud of despair settles in. Outside of Christ, a sour experience always tends to pessimism. It was so in the world when Jesus came. It is still so today.

But the dew of youth is incurably hopeful. There is an effervescent expectation that is naturally and magnificently borne in youth and retained in Christ. In every winter, when the fields are bleak, and the cold gust goes whistling through the trees, there lies the hope that the flowers will spring again. In every spring there is the hope of summer. In every summer there is the hope of harvest. It is alive in nature and alive in youth. Those who are blind to it shall reap, at best, a dreary monotone existence. To live is the rarest thing in the world. Most people exist, that is all. –Oscar Wilde.

The rest shall be brightly effected with a hope that…

…Heals Our Infirmities

Our bodies are destined for the grave and have no hope for renewal in this life. It is our minds that carry our greatest infirmities. The impotent man of 38 years at Bethesda could only utter a hopeless complaint when Christ asked him, …Wilt thou be made whole? –John 5:6. Upon the wake of his new day, a new remedy was given to him—… Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee –John 5:14. What could be worse than being a cripple for years? A mind that is beset by a doleful indulgence in the sorrows of this world. Age sets in when we have more memories of the past than hope for tomorrow. It is disappointing when folks grow old and have no vision for tomorrow, but it is a disaster to behold youth that are plagued by its crippling effects. Many grope aimlessly through life’s various trials, stupefied by the lack of blessedness. The noonday sun has evaporated the dew of their youth and the only praise that they can muster is culminated from a handful of yesterday’s pleasantries. A new attitude must be birthed by the dew of a new morning.

…Humbles Our Pursuits

Verily, verily, I say unto thee, When thou wast young, thou girdedst thyself, and walkedst whither thou wouldest: but when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not. –John 21:18. When we are young, we can overcome in the strength of our youth. As age takes its course, we will find a different alternative: victory through surrender.

…I have written unto you, young men, because ye are strong, and the word of God abideth in you, and ye have overcome the wicked one. –1 John 2:14. The world entices us to selfish living. Youth are often subject to schools of learning that teach them to “be all that you can be”. There is a major focus on self-enhancement and preparation for the future. This may prepare them in a ‘survival of the fittest’ world but will leave them destitute when the strength and prowess of youth has departed.

For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever. –1 John 2:16-17. Overcoming evil with good is the Biblical antidote for channeling youthful energies. Whether it is the lust within or the longing without, hope is conceived by planting a seed of kindness in the life of another. The pursuit of pleasure and lieu of leisure will always disappoint its recipient and leave him in a valley of despair deeper than when he began. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth … He putteth his mouth in the dust; if so be there may be hope. –Lamentations 3:27-29. We are created to work in God’s vineyard and those who have an appetite for it will reap in hope of its youthful reward.

…Hallows Our Trials

For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope... –Romans 8:24. How often we can relate to Job in his pain. But before his pain had received an ounce of retribution, the healing streams began to flow as Job reverenced his Creator. When we can acknowledge that God is perfect in all the trials He allows, we then learn to worship in the temple not made with hands and disregard the frailties of the body. To sit down at the feet of Christ ignites a youthful spark that radiates the spirit within and conceives hope. The dew of youth then becomes our portion as Christ imparts eternal life and eternal youth to us. From the hour of the grave and through eternity we shall be young and bid defiance to weariness and death if we are living in the morning light of Jesus Christ. Heaven is a place of perpetual youth, and just like the light of the sun is reflected on the moon, so likewise the light of Christ is reflected on His bride. She is clean and young, …a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing… –Ephesians 5:27. Blessed is the venerable saint who arrives at the portals of heaven in such a condition.

你的少年时光如清晨的露水。诗篇 110:3

青春有许多方面并不美德。我们这个时代的许多年轻人，很早就经历了麻木冷漠、鲁莽轻率的时期。年轻时所作的决定，常常为余生奠定基础。那个年轻的小儿子浪子要求提前支取自己的产业，随后便放荡度日，把产业挥霍一空。有个年轻的底拿离开父亲的家，……出去，要看看那地的女子。——创世记 34:1。在那里，她接触到当地的异教青年男子，酿成一场血腥屠杀，使雅各在那地成为臭名昭著的人。许多愚昧的年轻人种下狂风，收获的却是灾祸。那些缺乏坚定原则、又没有父母权柄引导的人，极易遭遇属灵的船难。

有些私欲对年轻人的伤害胜过对年长者，年轻人受劝要逃避这些私欲。（——参见提摩太后书 2:22）所罗门从窗棂向外观看，见愚蒙人内，见少年人中，分明有一个无知的少年人。——箴言 7:6-7。那年轻人一心追求看似美好的事物…………直等箭穿他的肝；他如同雀鸟急入网罗，却不知是自丧己命。——箴言 7:23。我们可以考察罗波安、暗嫩、拿答和亚比户等人的年轻岁月中所犯的恶行，以及无数其他人的例子。我们周围也不乏现代的例子：轻浮的年轻人充满愚行。

但年轻人不该受人轻看。不可叫人小看你年轻；总要在言语、行为、爱心、信心、清洁上，都作信徒的榜样。——提摩太前书 4:12。事实上，神通常拣选年轻人作祂传扬福音的器皿。品格高尚的约瑟，十七岁时蒙神差遣到埃及，为要保全生命（——参见创世记 45:5）。米利暗十二岁时，守在那位将来要拯救整个犹太民族的人身边，并设法让自己的母亲约基别作婴儿摩西的乳母。大卫年轻时被差去鼓励军中的弟兄。他遭兄长轻视：……我知道你的骄傲，和你心里的恶意……——撒母耳记上 17:28。他被扫罗拒绝：……你不能去与那非利士人战斗；因为你年纪太轻……——撒母耳记上 17:33。他被歌利亚嘲笑：……你拿着杖到我这里来，我岂是狗呢？……——撒母耳记上 17:43。然而，当神拣选他作全以色列的王时，他们的轻蔑全都落了空。

约西亚、以赛亚、耶利米、但以理、马利亚，以及主的门徒，都承继了这些高尚的青年志向；他们都选择在年少时记念造他们的主。但他们并非天真地想在人生中谋得一席之地，而是鲜明地显明了年轻人如何寻求效法主的形象。

我们无需长久凝视基督的品格，就会发现……

……你的少年时光如清晨的露水

诗篇 110 可能是旧约中被引用最多的经文。这幅关于弥赛亚的修辞画像，呈现出一个鲜明的美德，供我们瞻仰。基督作为亘古常在者，在《启示录》中被描写为头与发皆白，如白羊毛，如雪……——启示录 1:14；然而这里描绘的祂却永远年轻，坐在神的右边（——参见诗篇 110:1）。那里不会有年老带来的疲倦，因为基督是晨星。神的宝座周围，永远是清晨。那些竭力效法祂的人，也会映照出这美德，因为耶稣的光就是青春之光。

诗篇作者描写弥赛亚时，借用了清晨露水的自然之美（——参见诗篇 110:3）。露水这个意象把我们的目光从天上带回，使我们眼前显出一幅我们居住的地上景象。天上没有黑夜，没有冷热变化，也不需要太阳照亮白昼，因此……没有露水。露水属于大地；凡肯俯身观察的人，都会看见整齐如列队的青草闪闪发光，仿佛嵌满万千颗钻石。经过漫长的黑夜，露珠如泪珠般停留在花朵的眼中；当第一缕晨光到来，花朵欢喜得仿佛流泪。走过低矮草木的人，双脚会被神所造的千百只轻柔之手洗濯。基督所象征的不是清晨的露水，而是青春的露水；这个意象还可以进一步延展。

青春是精力充沛的时期。有些人坐不住。他们通常喜欢与人交往，热爱社交活动。这既不是美德，也不是恶习，而是寻常的天性。随着岁月增长，有一种逐渐发展的力量会磨炼并调和灵魂。人生渐进，我们的眼光更清晰，思想更稳健，也就迈向更美好的事物。然而，当我们越过中年顶峰，双脚沿着斜坡向下走时，那曾经横冲直撞的汹涌体力，便只能珍藏在往事的记忆中。对许多人来说，回忆往日强健的岁月，是他们能找到的最亲切的慰藉。

但基督并未呼召我们留恋过去，也没有要我们忧伤地怀念年轻时的“活力”。今天许多人哀叹自己已经失去了干劲。他们对更高远的事物毫无异象，比起青春的露水，他们喝一罐激浪汽水更能提振精神。他们更受回忆往事、追忆过去事件的鼓舞，而不是前方摆在眼前的盼望。

年岁增长并不妨碍人得着青春的露水。亘古常在者仍在金灯台中间行走。约翰看见祂的头与发……白如羊毛，白如雪……——启示录 1:14，所罗门却说……他的头发厚密，黑如乌鸦。——雅歌 5:11。年岁或许会夺去我们的体力和听力，然而……耶和华的膀臂并非缩短，不能拯救；耳朵并非发沉，不能听见。——以赛亚书 59:1。祂已经为我们保全青春的露水，并邀请我们来领受。问题不在于身体日渐衰败，而在于心灵日渐衰退。年老的祸患主要在于心灵随着身体一同衰退。

人生并不会随着岁月增长而变得贫乏，也不会在青春的魅力消逝时便不再高尚。如果我们来到世上只是为了经历欢乐，那么青春浪漫的消退就会令人痛苦不堪。但神为祂的儿女设定的目标远不止是让他们活力充沛地“做事”。我们被差到世上来学习。我们在世所分得的年日，都是为了受教；我们学到最深刻、最持久的功课，并非来自青春洋溢的浪漫，而是在坚忍地尽本分、平静地接受自身限制、耐心地担起每日的重担，以及向弟兄伸出援手时学到的。这些为我们提供了真正培养基督徒品格的机会，也是道德高尚的根基。基督劳苦，……不要为那必坏的食物劳力，要为那存到永生的食物劳力……——约翰福音 6:27，并在三十三年中完成了祂在世上的使命。但祂坐在父的右边时，青春的露水并未消散。

因此，我们得出结论：这种青春活力不是靠力量得着的，而是……

……盼望

但基督献了一次永远的赎罪祭，就坐在神的右边。从此等候仇敌成了祂的脚凳。——希伯来书 10:12-13。

我们如今该如何想象这位基督？祂会不会疲惫不堪地躺在安乐椅上，仿佛已经受够了世上顽梗的人？祂是否忙着制作一本珍贵回忆剪贴簿？年长者往往就是如此，以至于心灵随着身体一同死去。

不但如此，就是在患难中也是欢欢喜喜的；因为知道患难生忍耐，忍耐生老练，老练生盼望。——罗马书 5:3-4。有时我们会怀疑这段经文是否属实。凡是上了年纪的人，都能作证自己曾有过糟糕的经历，随后感到绝望。我们每个人都曾在配偶、子女或教会关系中经历令人失望的事，之后挥之不去的绝望阴云便笼罩心头。离开基督，令人失望的经历总会使人倾向悲观。耶稣降世时，世上的情形就是如此；今天仍然如此。

但青春的露水带着无法根除的盼望。青春天然地蕴含着一种活泼而美妙的期待；在基督里，这期待得以保留。每逢冬天，田野一片萧瑟，寒风呼啸着穿过树林，心中仍有盼望：花朵会再次绽放。每逢春天，就有对夏天的盼望；每逢夏天，就有对收成的盼望。盼望活在自然中，也活在青春中。对盼望视而不见的人，至多只能收获沉闷单调的人生。活着是世上最稀有的事。大多数人只是存在，仅此而已。——奥斯卡·王尔德。

其余的人则会因盼望而明亮起来，这盼望……

……医治我们的软弱

我们的身体注定归于坟墓，在今生没有更新的盼望。我们最大的软弱在于心思意念。那位在毕士大病了三十八年的瘫子，基督问他……你愿意痊愈吗？——约翰福音 5:6。他只能发出绝望的抱怨。当他迎来新的一天时，基督赐给他新的医治之道——……你已经痊愈了，不要再犯罪，恐怕你遭遇的更加严重。——约翰福音 5:14。有什么会比多年残疾更糟？那就是沉溺于世间哀伤的心。每当我们对过去的记忆多过对明日的盼望，衰老便开始了。人们年老之后对明日毫无异象，令人失望；但看见年轻人也受这种使人瘫痪的影响所困，更是一场灾难。许多人在生命的种种试炼中漫无目的地摸索，因缺乏福乐而麻木。正午的太阳蒸发了他们青春的露水，他们唯一能发出的赞美，也不过是从昨日少许欢愉中拼凑而来。新清晨的露水必须孕育出新的态度。

……使我们的追求谦卑

我实实在在地告诉你，你年少的时候，自己束上带子，随意往来；但年老的时候，你要伸出手来，别人要把你束上，带你到不愿意去的地方。——约翰福音 21:18。年轻时，我们能靠着青春的力量得胜。随着年岁增长，我们会发现另一种途径：借着降服而得胜。

……我写信给你们少年人，因为你们刚强，神的道常存在你们心里，你们也胜了那恶者。——约翰一书 2:14。世界诱惑我们自私地生活。年轻人常常要接受那些教他们“尽你所能做到最好”的学校教育。教育着重于自我提升和为未来作准备。在“适者生存”的世界里，这或许能帮助他们预备自己；但当青春的力量与本领消逝时，他们就会一无所有。

因为凡世界上的事，就像肉体的情欲、眼目的情欲，并今生的骄傲，都不是从父来的，乃是从世界来的。这世界和其上的情欲都要过去；惟独遵行神旨意的，是永远常存。——约翰一书 2:16-17。以善胜恶，是圣经所给的解方，能引导年轻人的活力。无论是内心的私欲，还是外在的渴求，只要在他人的生命中种下仁慈的种子，盼望便会萌生。追逐享乐、贪图闲暇，总会令追求者失望，使他陷入比起初更深的绝望谷底。人在幼年负轭，这原是好的……他当口贴尘埃，或者有指望。——耶利米哀歌 3:27-29。我们受造是要在神的葡萄园里劳作；凡有心投入其中的人，都会怀着盼望，收获青春的奖赏。

……使我们的试炼成圣

我们得救是在乎盼望；只是所见的盼望不是盼望……——罗马书 8:24。我们多么常能体会约伯的痛苦。然而，在他的痛苦尚未得到丝毫补偿之前，疗愈的溪流便已开始流淌，因为约伯敬畏他的造物主。当我们承认神在祂所容许的一切试炼中都是完全的，就学会在非人手所造的圣殿里敬拜，不再看重身体的脆弱。坐在基督脚前，会点燃青春的火花，照亮内里的灵，并孕育盼望。基督将永生和永恒的青春赐给我们，青春的露水便成为我们的分。自坟墓的时刻起，直到永恒，我们都将年轻；若我们活在耶稣基督清晨的光中，就能向疲倦和死亡夸胜。天堂是永恒青春之地；正如太阳的光反映在月亮上，基督的光也照耀在祂的新妇身上。她是圣洁而年轻的，……作个荣耀的教会，毫无玷污、皱纹等类的病……——以弗所书 5:27。有福了，那位德高望重的圣徒如此抵达天堂的门口。

Thou hast the dew of thy youth. Psalm 110:3

There are many aspects of youth which are not virtuous. Many youth of our day experience an early season of callused carelessness and casualty. Often decisions that are made in youthful years set the foundation for the rest of their lives. It was a the younger prodigal brother that asked for an early draw on his inheritance then went and wasted it on riotous living. It was a young Dinah who wandered from her father’s house and …went out to see the daughters of the land –Genesis 34:1. There, she was exposed to the heathen young men of the land and occasioned a bloody massacre, leaving Jacob as a stench in the land. Many foolish young people have sown to the wind and reaped the havoc thereof. Those that are void of solid principles and parental authority are at high risk for spiritual shipwreck.

There are particular lusts that inflict youth more so than the aged, and the young are exhorted to flee them. (–see 2 Timothy 2:22) Solomon looked through his window casement, And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding -Proverbs 7:6-7. The young man was in heartfelt pursuit of that which appeared lovely… [Un]Till a dart [struck] through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life –Proverbs 7:23. We could examine the vices from the youthful lives of Rehoboam, Amnon, Nadab and Abihu, and countless others. We also find no lack of modern, folly-filled examples about us fulfilled by frivolous youth.

But youth are not meant to be despised. Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity –1 Timothy 4:12. In fact, God generally chooses the youth as the instruments of His propagation. Joseph, of sterling character, was sent by God into Egypt at the age of 17 to preserve life (–see Genesis 45:5). Miriam, at the age of twelve, stood post over the future deliverer of the entire Jewish nation and secured her own mother, Jochebed, to be the nurse of the baby Moses. David, as a youth, was sent to encourage his brethren in the army. He was despised by his brothers: …I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart… –1 Samuel 17:28. He was rejected by Saul: …Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth… –1 Samuel 17:33. He was scorned by Goliath: …Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves… –1 Samuel 17:43. But their contempt was all for naught when he was chosen by God to be king over all Israel.

These noble youthful ambitions were followed by Josiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Mary, and the disciples of the Lord, all who chose to remember their Creator in the days of their youth. But these were not naive specimens seeking to secure their place in life, they were graphic examples of youth who were seeking to imitate the image of their Lord.

We need not gaze long into the character of Christ before we find…

...Thou hast the dew of thy youth

Psalm 110 is perhaps the most referred-to scripture in the Old Testament. This rhetorical portrait of the Messiah reveals a vivid virtue for us to behold. Christ, as the Ancient of days, was described in the Revelation having His head and His hairs ... white like wool, as white as snow… –Revelation 1:14, yet, here He is depicted as eternally young, as He sits at the right hand of God (–see Psalm 110:1). No weariness of age can enter there, for Christ is the Morning Star. It is perpetual morning around the throne of God. Those saints who are following hard after His likeness will also reflect this virtue, for the light of Jesus is the light of youth.

The psalmist, describing the Messiah, draws from the natural beauty of the morning dew (–see Psalm 110:3). The thought of dew calls us back from the heavens and unveils before us a portrait of this earth on which we dwell. In heaven there is no night, no change of heat and cold, no need of the sun to light up the day and consequently… no dew. The nature of dew belongs to the terrestrial, where everyone who will but stoop to observe it will behold a uniformed regiment of grass sparkling as if embedded with a myriad of diamonds. After a long night of darkness, the dewdrops, like tears, stand in the eyes of the flowers as they weep for joy at the advent of the first morning sunbeam. Those who walk through the lowly vegetation will have their feet washed by a thousand caressing hands of God’s design. Christ is not depicted as the dew of the morning but as the dew of youth, and the imagery is stretched further.

Youth is the season of abounding energy. Some cannot sit still. They are generally interpersonal creatures who love social activity. This is neither a virtue nor a vice. Rather, it is nominal nature. There is a progressive strain in advancing years that tames and tempers the soul. As life progresses, there is a clearer vision and a steadier thought, and we rise to better things. But when the mid-life summit has been crossed and the feet are traveling downward on the slope, that tumultuous rush of bodily energy that plowed through anything becomes enshrined with memories of the past. It is the closest comfort many can find to the bygone days of their strength.

But Christ has not called us to foster a fondness for the past nor a wistful longing for the “DO” of our youth. So many today sadly lament that their ‘get-up-and-go’ has got up and went. These have no vision for higher things and are more energized by a can of Mountain Dew than the Dew of Youth. They are more inspired by a trip down memory lane and reminiscing events of the past than of the hope that lies before them.

Age is no hindrance to securing the dew of youth. The Ancient of Days still rides forth among the golden candlesticks. While John beheld His hairs ... white like wool, as white as snow… –Revelation 1:14, yet Solomon declares …his locks are bushy, and black as a raven –Song of Solomon 5:11. While age may steal our strength and hearing, …the LORD’S hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear: –Isaiah 59:1. He has secured the dew of youth and invites us to partake. The problem is not found in our deteriorating body but in a spiritually declining mind. The bane of old age predominately sets in when the mind follows the body.

It is not that life grows poorer as it advances or ceases to be noble when the charm of youth has faded. If we were placed here only to experience joy, the dying out of youthful romance would be terrible. God had a much greater end in view for His children than to just be vibrant ‘doers’. We are sent here to learn. Our allotted years upon earth are all meant to be a schooling, and it is not in the bright romance of youth that we learn the best and most abiding lessons. It is in the dogged doing of our duty, the quiet acceptance of our limitations, the patient carrying of our daily burden, and in the stretching out of a helping hand to our brother. These afford us the true opportunities for Christian culture and are the roots of ethical nobility. Christ labored …not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life… –John 6:27, and He finished His earthly task in 33 years. But the dew of youth did not dissipate as He sat down at the right hand of His Father.

Thus, we conclude that this youthfulness will not be secured by strength, but by…

...Hope

But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God; From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. –Hebrews 10:12-13.

How shall we picture this Christ now? Reclining in an easy chair, all worn out from His experience with the stubborn people of this earth? Is He busy putting together a scrap book of precious memories? This is too often the position of the aged and so their mind dies with their bodies.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope –Romans 5:3-4. At times, we wonder if this scripture can be true. Anyone with any age on their bones can testify to a poor experience and the subsequent feelings of hopelessness following. As people, we have all faced disappointing experiences with a spouse, a child, or a church relationship after which a nagging cloud of despair settles in. Outside of Christ, a sour experience always tends to pessimism. It was so in the world when Jesus came. It is still so today.

But the dew of youth is incurably hopeful. There is an effervescent expectation that is naturally and magnificently borne in youth and retained in Christ. In every winter, when the fields are bleak, and the cold gust goes whistling through the trees, there lies the hope that the flowers will spring again. In every spring there is the hope of summer. In every summer there is the hope of harvest. It is alive in nature and alive in youth. Those who are blind to it shall reap, at best, a dreary monotone existence. To live is the rarest thing in the world. Most people exist, that is all. –Oscar Wilde.

The rest shall be brightly effected with a hope that…

…Heals Our Infirmities

Our bodies are destined for the grave and have no hope for renewal in this life. It is our minds that carry our greatest infirmities. The impotent man of 38 years at Bethesda could only utter a hopeless complaint when Christ asked him, …Wilt thou be made whole? –John 5:6. Upon the wake of his new day, a new remedy was given to him—… Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee –John 5:14. What could be worse than being a cripple for years? A mind that is beset by a doleful indulgence in the sorrows of this world. Age sets in when we have more memories of the past than hope for tomorrow. It is disappointing when folks grow old and have no vision for tomorrow, but it is a disaster to behold youth that are plagued by its crippling effects. Many grope aimlessly through life’s various trials, stupefied by the lack of blessedness. The noonday sun has evaporated the dew of their youth and the only praise that they can muster is culminated from a handful of yesterday’s pleasantries. A new attitude must be birthed by the dew of a new morning.

…Humbles Our Pursuits

Verily, verily, I say unto thee, When thou wast young, thou girdedst thyself, and walkedst whither thou wouldest: but when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not. –John 21:18. When we are young, we can overcome in the strength of our youth. As age takes its course, we will find a different alternative: victory through surrender.

…I have written unto you, young men, because ye are strong, and the word of God abideth in you, and ye have overcome the wicked one. –1 John 2:14. The world entices us to selfish living. Youth are often subject to schools of learning that teach them to “be all that you can be”. There is a major focus on self-enhancement and preparation for the future. This may prepare them in a ‘survival of the fittest’ world but will leave them destitute when the strength and prowess of youth has departed.

For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever. –1 John 2:16-17. Overcoming evil with good is the Biblical antidote for channeling youthful energies. Whether it is the lust within or the longing without, hope is conceived by planting a seed of kindness in the life of another. The pursuit of pleasure and lieu of leisure will always disappoint its recipient and leave him in a valley of despair deeper than when he began. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth … He putteth his mouth in the dust; if so be there may be hope. –Lamentations 3:27-29. We are created to work in God’s vineyard and those who have an appetite for it will reap in hope of its youthful reward.

…Hallows Our Trials

For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope... –Romans 8:24. How often we can relate to Job in his pain. But before his pain had received an ounce of retribution, the healing streams began to flow as Job reverenced his Creator. When we can acknowledge that God is perfect in all the trials He allows, we then learn to worship in the temple not made with hands and disregard the frailties of the body. To sit down at the feet of Christ ignites a youthful spark that radiates the spirit within and conceives hope. The dew of youth then becomes our portion as Christ imparts eternal life and eternal youth to us. From the hour of the grave and through eternity we shall be young and bid defiance to weariness and death if we are living in the morning light of Jesus Christ. Heaven is a place of perpetual youth, and just like the light of the sun is reflected on the moon, so likewise the light of Christ is reflected on His bride. She is clean and young, …a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing… –Ephesians 5:27. Blessed is the venerable saint who arrives at the portals of heaven in such a condition.

Du har din ungdoms dagg. Psaltaren 110:3

Det finns många aspekter av ungdom som inte är dygdiga. Många unga i vår tid upplever tidigt en period av förhärdad likgiltighet och förödelse. Ofta lägger beslut som fattas under ungdomsåren grunden för resten av livet. Det var den yngre förlorade sonen som bad att få ut sitt arv i förtid och sedan gick bort och slösade bort det genom ett utsvävande liv. Det var den unga Dina som vandrade bort från sin fars hus och …gick ut för att se landets döttrar – Första Moseboken 34:1. Där utsattes hon för landets hedniska unga män och blev orsaken till en blodig massaker, så att Jakob blev en stank i landet. Många dåraktiga unga har sått i vinden och fått skörda förödelsen därav. De som saknar fasta principer och föräldrars auktoritet löper stor risk att lida andligt skeppsbrott.

Det finns särskilda lustar som drabbar unga mer än äldre, och de unga uppmanas att fly från dem. (–se 2 Timoteusbrevet 2:22) Salomo såg ut genom sitt fönster, och bland de enfaldiga såg jag, bland de unga urskilde jag en yngling utan förstånd – Ordspråksboken 7:6–7. Den unge mannen jagade ivrigt efter det som verkade ljuvligt … [t]ills en pil genomborrade hans lever; likt en fågel som skyndar till snaran utan att veta att det gäller hans liv – Ordspråksboken 7:23. Vi skulle kunna undersöka lasterna i Rehabeams, Amnons, Nadabs och Abihus ungdomsliv, liksom hos otaliga andra. Vi finner också ingen brist på moderna, dårskapsfyllda exempel omkring oss, där tanklösa unga står för dem.

Men unga ska inte föraktas. Låt ingen förakta dig för att du är ung, utan var ett föredöme för de troende i ord och gärning, i kärlek, tro och renhet – 1 Timoteusbrevet 4:12. Gud väljer faktiskt i allmänhet de unga som redskap för att föra sitt verk vidare. Josef, med sin enastående karaktär, sändes av Gud till Egypten vid 17 års ålder för att bevara liv (–se Första Moseboken 45:5). Mirjam, som var tolv år, stod vakt över den blivande befriare som skulle rädda hela det judiska folket och såg till att hennes egen mor, Jokebed, blev den lille Moses amma. David sändes som ung för att uppmuntra sina bröder i hären. Han föraktades av sina bröder: …Jag känner ditt övermod och ditt hjärtas ondska … – Första Samuelsboken 17:28. Han avvisades av Saul: …Du kan inte gå mot den här filistén och strida med honom, för du är bara en pojke … – Första Samuelsboken 17:33. Han hånades av Goliat: …Är jag en hund, eftersom du kommer mot mig med käppar … – Första Samuelsboken 17:43. Men deras förakt var förgäves när Gud utvalde honom till kung över hela Israel.

Dessa ädla ungdomsambitioner följdes av Josia, Jesaja, Jeremia, Daniel, Maria och Herrens lärjungar, som alla valde att komma ihåg sin Skapare i sin ungdom. Men de var inga naiva personer som försökte säkra sin plats i livet; de var tydliga exempel på unga som strävade efter att efterlikna sin Herres bild.

Vi behöver inte betrakta Kristi karaktär länge förrän vi finner …

… Du har din ungdoms dagg

Psaltaren 110 är kanske det skriftställe som oftast hänvisas till i Gamla testamentet. Denna retoriska skildring av Messias visar oss en levande dygd att betrakta. Kristus, den Evige, beskrivs i Uppenbarelseboken med huvud och hår … vita som ull, vita som snö … – Uppenbarelseboken 1:14, men här skildras han som evigt ung, när han sitter på Guds högra sida (–se Psaltaren 110:1). Ålderns trötthet kan inte nå dit, för Kristus är morgonstjärnan. Det råder en ständig morgon kring Guds tron. De heliga som helhjärtat följer hans likhet kommer också att återspegla denna dygd, för Jesu ljus är ungdomens ljus.

Psalmisten hämtar, när han beskriver Messias, en bild från morgondaggens naturliga skönhet (–se Psaltaren 110:3). Tanken på dagg för oss tillbaka från himlen och visar oss en bild av jorden där vi bor. I himlen finns ingen natt, inga växlingar mellan värme och kyla, inget behov av solen för att lysa upp dagen och följaktligen … ingen dagg. Dagg hör till det jordiska, där var och en som böjer sig ner för att betrakta den får se ett ordnat led av grässtrån som glittrar som om de vore besatta med otaliga diamanter. Efter en lång, mörk natt står daggdropparna likt tårar i blommornas ögon, när de gråter av glädje över den första morgonsolstrålens ankomst. De som går genom den låga växtligheten får fötterna tvättade av tusen smekande händer, skapade av Gud. Kristus skildras inte som morgonens dagg utan som ungdomens dagg, och bilden vidgas ytterligare.

Ungdomen är en tid av överflödande energi. En del kan inte sitta stilla. De är i regel sociala varelser som älskar umgänge. Detta är varken en dygd eller en last. Det är snarare en del av den mänskliga naturen. Med åren uppstår en fortskridande påfrestning som tämjer och mildrar själen. Allteftersom livet går vidare blir synen klarare och tanken stadigare, och vi strävar efter bättre ting. Men när vi har passerat medelålderns höjdpunkt och fötterna går nedför sluttningen, blir den våldsamma rusning av kroppslig energi som en gång plöjde sig fram genom allt något som bevaras i minnen från det förflutna. För många är detta den närmaste tröst de kan finna för de svunna dagar då de hade sin styrka.

Men Kristus har inte kallat oss att vårda en förkärlek för det förflutna eller en vemodig längtan efter ungdomens ”ork”. Så många i dag beklagar sorgset att deras ”driv” har gett sig av. De har ingen vision om högre ting och får mer energi av en burk Mountain Dew än av ungdomens dagg. De inspireras mer av en nostalgisk tillbakablick och minnen av det förflutna än av hoppet som ligger framför dem.

Ålder är inget hinder för att få del av ungdomens dagg. Den Evige rider fortfarande fram bland de gyllene ljusstakarna. Johannes såg hans hår … vitt som ull, vitt som snö … – Uppenbarelseboken 1:14, men Salomo förklarar ändå: …hans lockar är yviga och svarta som korpen – Höga visan 5:11. Även om åldern kan beröva oss vår styrka och hörsel, är …HERRENS hand inte för kort, så att den inte kan frälsa, och hans öra inte dövt, så att det inte kan höra – Jesaja 59:1. Han har säkrat ungdomens dagg och inbjuder oss att ta del av den. Problemet finns inte i vår kropp som förfaller, utan i ett sinne som andligen går tillbaka. Ålderdomens gissel slår framför allt till när sinnet följer kroppen.

Det är inte så att livet blir fattigare medan det fortskrider eller upphör att vara ädelt när ungdomens charm har bleknat. Om vi bara hade satts här för att uppleva glädje, skulle det vara fruktansvärt när ungdomens romantik dör ut. Gud hade ett mycket större mål för sina barn än att de bara skulle vara livskraftiga ”görare”. Vi är sända hit för att lära. De år vi fått tilldelade här på jorden är alla avsedda att vara en skolgång, och det är inte ungdomens ljusa romantik som lär oss de bästa och mest bestående läxorna. Det är när vi envist gör vår plikt, stilla accepterar våra begränsningar, tålmodigt bär vår dagliga börda och sträcker ut en hjälpande hand till vår broder. Detta ger oss verkliga möjligheter till kristen fostran och utgör rötterna till etisk ädelhet. Kristus arbetade …inte för den mat som förgås, utan för den mat som består till evigt liv … – Johannesevangeliet 6:27, och han fullbordade sin jordiska uppgift på 33 år. Men ungdomens dagg försvann inte när han satte sig på sin Faders högra sida.

Vi drar alltså slutsatsen att denna ungdomlighet inte vinns genom styrka, utan genom …

… Hopp

Men denne har framburit ett enda offer för synderna för all framtid och sedan satt sig på Guds högra sida. Där väntar han härefter på att hans fiender ska läggas som en fotpall under hans fötter. – Hebreerbrevet 10:12–13.

Hur ska vi föreställa oss Kristus nu? Ligger han tillbakalutad i en fåtölj, helt utsliten efter sina erfarenheter med jordens hårdnackade folk? Är han upptagen med att sätta ihop en klippbok med kära minnen? Alltför ofta är detta de äldres tillstånd, och därför dör deras sinne med kroppen.

Och inte bara det, vi gläder oss också mitt i våra lidanden, eftersom vi vet att lidandet ger tålamod, tålamodet fasthet och fastheten hopp – Romarbrevet 5:3–4. Ibland undrar vi om detta skriftställe kan vara sant. Alla som hunnit bli äldre kan vittna om smärtsamma erfarenheter och de efterföljande känslorna av hopplöshet. Som människor har vi alla haft nedslående erfarenheter med en make eller maka, ett barn eller en församlingsrelation, efter vilka ett envist förtvivlans moln lägger sig. Utanför Kristus leder en bitter erfarenhet alltid till pessimism. Så var det i världen när Jesus kom. Så är det fortfarande i dag.

Men ungdomens dagg är obotligt hoppfull. Det finns en sprudlande förväntan som naturligt och storslaget föds i ungdomen och bevaras i Kristus. Under varje vinter, när fälten ligger kala och kalla vindbyar viner genom träden, finns hoppet om att blommorna ska spira igen. Varje vår rymmer hoppet om sommar. Varje sommar rymmer hoppet om skörd. Det lever i naturen och i ungdomen. De som är blinda för det får i bästa fall skörda en dyster och enformig tillvaro. Att leva är det sällsyntaste i världen. De flesta existerar, det är allt. – Oscar Wilde.

De övriga ska påverkas strålande av ett hopp som …

… Botar våra svagheter

Våra kroppar är bestämda för graven och har inget hopp om förnyelse i detta liv. Det är våra sinnen som bär på våra största svagheter. Den lame mannen som varit vid Betesda i 38 år kunde bara yttra ett hopplöst klagomål när Kristus frågade honom: …Vill du bli frisk? – Johannesevangeliet 5:6. När hans nya dag grydde fick han ett nytt råd: …Se, du har blivit frisk. Synda inte mer, så att inte något värre drabbar dig – Johannesevangeliet 5:14. Vad kan vara värre än att vara lam i åratal? Ett sinne som plågas av att vältra sig i denna världens sorger. Åldern slår till när vi har fler minnen av det förflutna än hopp för morgondagen. Det är nedslående när människor blir gamla utan att ha någon vision för morgondagen, men det är en katastrof att se unga som plågas av dess förlamande verkningar. Många trevar planlöst genom livets olika prövningar, förlamade av bristen på salighet. Middagssolen har förångat ungdomens dagg, och det enda beröm de kan uppbringa kommer från en handfull gårdagens glädjeämnen. En ny inställning måste födas av en ny morgons dagg.

… Ödmjukar våra strävanden

Sannerligen, sannerligen säger jag dig: När du var ung, klädde du dig själv och gick dit du ville. Men när du blir gammal ska du sträcka ut dina händer, och en annan ska klä dig och föra dig dit du inte vill. – Johannesevangeliet 21:18. När vi är unga kan vi övervinna genom ungdomens styrka. När åldern gör sitt kommer vi att finna ett annat alternativ: seger genom kapitulation.

…Jag har skrivit till er unga män, eftersom ni är starka och Guds ord förblir i er och ni har övervunnit den onde. – Första Johannesbrevet 2:14. Världen lockar oss till ett själviskt liv. Unga får ofta gå i skolor som lär dem att ”bli allt ni kan bli”. Det läggs stor vikt vid att utveckla sig själv och förbereda sig för framtiden. Det kan förbereda dem för en värld där ”den starkaste överlever”, men lämnar dem utblottade när ungdomens styrka och kraft har försvunnit.

Ty allt som finns i världen – köttets begär och ögonens begär och högmod över livets goda – kommer inte från Fadern utan från världen. Och världen går under, med sina begär, men den som gör Guds vilja består för evigt. – Första Johannesbrevet 2:16–17. Att övervinna det onda med det goda är Bibelns motgift för att kanalisera ungdomens krafter. Vare sig det gäller lusten inom oss eller längtan efter det som är utanför oss, föds hopp när vi sår ett frö av vänlighet i en annan människas liv. Jakten på njutning och valet av bekvämlighet kommer alltid att göra den som tar emot dem besviken och lämna honom i en djupare förtvivlans dal än den han började i. Det är gott för en man att bära ett ok i sin ungdom … Han lägger sin mun i stoftet; kanske finns det hopp. – Klagovisorna 3:27–29. Vi är skapade för att arbeta i Guds vingård, och de som har aptit på det kommer att skörda i hopp om dess ungdomliga belöning.

… Helgar våra prövningar

Ty i hoppet är vi frälsta. Men ett hopp som man ser är inte något hopp … – Romarbrevet 8:24. Hur ofta kan vi inte känna igen oss i Jobs lidande. Men innan hans smärta hade fått minsta vedergällning började läkande strömmar flyta, när Job vördade sin Skapare. När vi kan erkänna att Gud är fullkomlig i alla prövningar han tillåter, lär vi oss då att tillbe i templet som inte är gjort av människohänder och bortse från kroppens skröplighet. Att sätta sig vid Kristi fötter tänder en ungdomlig gnista som strålar ut från anden inom oss och föder hopp. Ungdomens dagg blir då vår lott, när Kristus ger oss evigt liv och evig ungdom. Från gravens stund och genom evigheten ska vi vara unga och trotsa trötthet och död, om vi lever i Jesu Kristi morgonljus. Himlen är en plats av evig ungdom, och liksom solens ljus återspeglas i månen, så återspeglas också Kristi ljus i hans brud. Hon är ren och ung, …en härlig församling utan fläck eller skrynkla eller något sådant … – Efesierbrevet 5:27. Välsignat är det vördnadsvärda helgon som når himlens portar i ett sådant tillstånd.
